analysis.one_liner: Makes the expiring 2017 individual and small-business tax cuts permanent.
analysis.headline: Introduced September 20, 2022 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, the bill died there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, with all 120 cosponsors Republican.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have locked in, permanently, the individual and small-business parts of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act that were written to expire after 2025: lower income tax rates, a bigger standard deduction, a $2,000 child tax credit, a 20% deduction for owners of pass-through businesses, a doubled estate-tax exemption, and a higher alternative minimum tax exemption. It would also have made permanent the $10,000 cap on deducting state and local taxes. It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never moved again before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Middle-income families would keep real, continuing tax cuts — the larger standard deduction and the $2,000 child tax credit — rather than facing a scheduled 2025 tax increase. But the largest dollar gains go to the top: the 37% top rate applies above $600,000 of income, the alternative minimum tax exemption would not phase out until $1 million, owners of pass-through businesses (including law firms, real estate partnerships, and other high-income owners) keep a 20% deduction, and estates worth more than the doubled $10 million exemption escape the estate tax that would otherwise apply. Extending all of this reduces federal revenue for as long as the cuts last.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, pass-through owners, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: Continues the lower individual income tax rates and a roughly doubled standard deduction instead of letting them lapse at the end of 2025.
Keeps the $2,000 per-child tax credit (up to $1,400 of it refundable) in place permanently.
Makes permanent the 20% deduction for qualified business income of pass-through entities such as sole proprietorships, partnerships, and S corporations.
Doubles the estate and gift tax exemption to a $10 million base amount per person, shielding the largest estates from tax.

Restores tax-free treatment for student loans discharged on death or total and permanent disability, and expands 529 education savings accounts to cover elementary and secondary tuition, tutoring, testing, and therapies for students with disabilities.
Makes permanent the higher alternative minimum tax exemption, with the phase-out pushed to $1 million.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the cost: the 2017 law's individual provisions were scheduled to expire after 2025 precisely so their cost window would close, and making them permanent keeps that revenue off the books indefinitely — a burden that falls on future taxpayers through larger deficits or on programs funded from general revenue. Homeowners in high-tax states also keep the $10,000 limit on deducting state and local taxes, and larger families keep the repeal of the personal exemption deduction.

drawbacks.text: The provisions were written to expire after 2025 so the 2017 law's official cost window would close; making them permanent keeps the tax cuts — and the revenue loss that came with them — on the books for good.

The largest permanent gains are concentrated at the top: the 37% rate applies above $600,000 of income, the alternative minimum tax exemption would not begin phasing out until $1 million, and the estate and gift tax exemption is doubled.

The bill locks in provisions that raise some people's taxes: the $10,000 cap on deducting state and local taxes, the repeal of the personal exemption deduction (which hit larger families), and the termination of miscellaneous itemized deductions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Middle-income families would genuinely keep lower taxes, a bigger standard deduction, and the child credit, and families with disabled children or student debt get real relief. But the design is skewed: the pieces that are most expensive to extend — the top rates, the pass-through deduction, the AMT change, and the doubled estate exemption — flow disproportionately to the highest earners and largest estates, and the whole package deepens deficits indefinitely. An honest supporter would have to admit the bill spends the most where households need it least.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, never receiving a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Vern Buchanan introduced the bill on September 20, 2022, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
It drew 120 cosponsors in its first weeks, every one of them a Republican.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 without the bill ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed for anyone's current taxes, since the provisions remain law through 2025 whether or not this passed. The main difference is that the expiration dates stayed on the books: Congress kept the option to revisit the tax cuts later, and the deficit was spared the permanent cost. High earners, pass-through owners, and large estates did not get their lower taxes locked in permanently.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Future taxpayers — the cuts weren't locked in

sides.party_line_note: All 120 cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill received no action in the committee run by Democrats, who held the House majority.

industries.note: Making the 20% qualified business income deduction permanent is a lasting tax cut for owners of partnerships, S corporations, and sole proprietorships — a group that includes many high earners in law, real estate, and finance alongside genuinely small businesses. The revenue cost is spread across all taxpayers.

The 37% top rate, the $1 million AMT phase-out, and the doubled estate-tax exemption concentrate the largest permanent dollar gains in the top brackets. The offsetting cost is forgone federal revenue borne broadly by everyone else.

industries.industry: Private K-12 schools and education service providers
industries.note: Expanding 529 accounts to cover private and religious school tuition, tutoring, testing, and educational therapies channels tax-advantaged savings toward these providers and benefits the families able to use them.
Making permanent the 60% limit on deductible cash gifts keeps the more generous deduction for donors that the 2017 law created, supporting nonprofit fundraising.

Making the $10,000 deduction cap permanent keeps the tax code limit on state and local tax deductibility, which residents of states with high income and property taxes — and those state governments that lean on them — argue discourages their tax structures. Other states with low taxes are unaffected.
